earlier_scan.source_named: Aimol, Chongom Damrengthang 2007. A descriptive grammar of Kom (grammar); also Kom, Karung Tarun 2009 (phonology) — per Glottolog; no online copy reachable

new_statements.quote: p.14: "The Kom language has twenty-seven principal phonemes. Out of the twenty-seven phonemes the number of segmental and suprasegmental phonemes are twenty-five and two respectively. [...] The two suprasegmental phonemes are level tone and falling tone." p.54: "Tone is one of the main characteristics of Tibeto-Burman language. [...] Kom has two tones as that of Manipuri has. Falling tone is marked by /ˋ/ and level tone which left unmarked." (examples: ten 'fishing net' vs tèn 'fishing net (male)', puŋ 'gong' vs pùŋ 'hour', in 'house' vs ìn 'fishing net (female)', tur 'push' vs tùr 'poison')
new_statements.citation: Aimol, Chongom Damrengthang. 2007. A descriptive grammar of Kom. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Canchipur. (Shodhganga hdl:10603/105232)
new_statements.locator: Ch. II sec. 2.0 'The phonological system', p. 14; sec. 2.4 'Tone', p. 54 (both pages checked against the page images)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and rendered PDF p.2 (printed p.14) and PDF p.41 (printed p.54) as images. p.14 reads exactly: "The Kom language has twenty-seven principal phonemes. Out of the twenty-seven phonemes the number of segmental and suprasegmental phonemes are twenty-five and two respectively. Segmental phonemes include nineteen consonants... and six vowels... The two suprasegmental phonemes are level tone and falling tone." followed by the classification (B) Supra-segmental phonemes a) Tones (2) i) Level tone ii) Falling tone. p.54, sec. 2.4 TONE: "Tone is one of the main characteristics of Tibeto-Burman language.... Kom has two tones as that of Manipuri has. Falling tone is marked by /`/ and level tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kom is described as a lexical tone language with a two-way tonal contrast on syllables (Aimol 2007 and Sucheta 1998: level vs falling; Kom 2009: high [slightly falling] vs low); the only suprasegmental phonemes recognised are the two tones. None of the three descriptions that treat Kom phonology mentions word stress or accent at all, either as contrastive or as predictable, so no stress-placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement). Concurring tonal statements: Kom, Karung Tarun 2009, ch.3 sec. 3.8.2, PDF p.47 (file kom2010_nehu/): "Kom is a tonal language. Tone plays a very important role in the language as the same word may mean two or three different things with the changing of the tone. There are two register tones in Kom at the lexical level. They are – (i) high tone (╱) and (ii) low tone (╲). High tone is a tone with high pitch falling slightly and low tone is a tone with low pitch." Sucheta 1998 sec. 4.1.5 p.83: "In Kom, there are two tones, one is level tone and the other one is considered as falling tone."
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is assigned per syllable/lexical item in citation forms (mono- and disyllabic minimal pairs). Aimol 2007 is based on the Khoirentak Khunou village variety (Churachandpur district); Kom 2009 describes 'standard Kom' = the Mongtung variety; both note village-level dialect variation but mutual intelligibility.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary descriptions are of Kom proper (kmm, komi1270), not the Kolhreng/Koireng variety. Aimol 2007 data: Khoirentak Khunou village (Churachandpur district). Kom 2009/2010 phonology: 'standard Kom', i.e. the Mongtung variety (audio Bible plus two elderly Mongtung speakers); its ch.4 treats Mantak and other village varieties. Glottolog's Shultz 1997 SIL-Cameroon item belongs to Kom of Cameroon (Grassfields), not this language.

sources.note: Nothing. Phonology chapter covers vowels, consonants, clusters, syllable (2.3) and tone (2.4): 27 phonemes of which two are suprasegmental, 'level tone and falling tone' (p.14); 'Kom has two tones as that of Manipuri has' (p.54). Ch.1 p.1: 'It is an agglutinative as well as tonal language.' No section or remark on stress/accent anywhere in ch.1-2 (scanned grep: stress/accent absent).

sources.citation: Kom, Karung Tarun. 2009 [degree 2010]. A description of the Kom speech with special emphasis on variation. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong (supervisor J. War). Shodhganga http://hdl.handle.net/10603/5505. Ch. 3 'Phonology of Kom' (50 pp., text layer).
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. Sec. 3.8.2 'Tones in Kom' (PDF p.47): 'Kom is a tonal language... There are two register tones in Kom at the lexical level. They are – (i) high tone and (ii) low tone. High tone is a tone with high pitch falling slightly and low tone is a tone with low pitch', with minimal pairs (thái 'edible'/thài 'oil', túi 'tasty'/tùi 'water'...). Describes 'standard Kom' = Mongtung variety. 'stress' occurs only inside quoted definitions (Schane, sonority).

sources.citation: Sucheta, Elangbam. 1998. A grammatical comparison of Manipuri, Kom, Paite and Tangkhul. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University. Shodhganga http://hdl.handle.net/10603/105206. Ch. IV 'Kom phonology' pp. 76-87 (image scan, scanned).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 4.1.5 'Supra-Segmental' (p.83): 'In Kom, there are two tones, one is level tone and the other one is considered as falling tone', with pairs be 'pulse'/bè 'pitcher', in 'house'/ìn 'fishing net'. Suprasegmentals = tones only (the parallel Manipuri chapter has tones + junctures).

sources.note: 'Pronunciation' paragraph (p.244) treats vowel interchange, aspirated nasals/liquids, final consonant voicing; says nothing about accent or tone for Kom (unlike some neighbouring sketches that state 'no information with regard to accents and tones').
